newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr slips again, but hint of base.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr slips again, but hint of base.

text.p: The Australian dollar laboured under corrective pressure for the third session in a row Wednesday, but at least found enough support to lift it from session lows by the close.

Traders said selling been heavy again through the morning as U.S. funds and Japanese names, amongst others, dumped long dollar positions, partly with the intention of cracking support at US$0.7850 and triggering stop-loss sales.
Aggressive buying from a Swiss bank and a burst of fund bids for AUD/Kiwi helped that bulwark hold, however, leading most dealers feeling the correction had found a base for the moment.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the currency had bowed to US$0.7861/66 from an early US$0.7875/80 and US$0.7900/05 late here Tuesday, but was up from the session trough of US$0.7848.
Traders said flows on both sides had been quite heavy but the actual liquidity of the market was poor as many banks were reluctant to quote decent spreads while prices were so volatile.
"There's bad stories going around about the losses some banks suffered in the pullback from 80 cents," said one. "It's made everyone nervous, whether they've taken a bath or not."
"Liquidity is awful as a result and nobody here is willing to take a punt on where the AUD's going next."

He felt support at US$0.7850 should provide a base for the near term given its performance today, while many chart watchers were expecting US$0.7835 to be as resilient as at the start of the month when it defeated a week of downside probes.
If it were to break, a retracement to US$0.7750 was on the cards, while bulls would have to recapture US$0.7910 to regain the ascendancy.

The dollar lost further ground on the crosses as both the mark and Swiss franc staged rallies of their own and Tokyo sold AUD/yen in size taking it down to 96.63/73 yen from 97.25/35 late here Tuesday and 1.3188/3204 marks from 1.3382/83.
In trade weighted terms the currency retreated to 60.6 from a previous 60.9 close.

The day's only data was of secondary importance but did support the upbeat outlook the Reserve Bank had taken on the economy last mnonth. The Westpac/Melbourne Institute leading index of economic activity jumped 1.4 points or 1.0 percent in January, and coincident index climbed 3.0 points or 1.7 percent.

"The strong rise in the index reinforces the upward trend evident in the previous three months and has pushed the smooth growth rate to four percent, its strongest pace since October 1994," said Westpac economics manager Bill Evans.
Traders reported some tension over rumours the Industrial Relations Commission (IRC) would issue its verdict on a major minimum wage case today.
The IRC later said no date had been set as yet and it would give advance warning of the timing.
The case is crucial to the outlook for monetary policy since the RBA has warned that if granted in full, it would raise wages growth sharply and greatly restrict potential employment growth.
Australia's main union body has asked for an immediate rise of 8.75 percent in award (minimum) wage rates plus A$20 a week, then two further A$20 rises in the next two years.
The government, on the orther hand, had proposed raising low-pay awards by A$8 a week each year for the next three years.

This was the outcome favoured by the RBA and anything much more than this would threaten to push up average weekly earnings -- which were already set to rise toward the bank's 4.5 percent pain threshold in the March quarter.
Thus a high outcome would tend to favour the dollar by further reducing the chance of a policy easing, while a low result would suggest some room still remained for a cut.
